## TL;DR

Reworked automated release emails around a short, notes-derived summary. Subjects now use the configured display name and version with a meaningful headline when the release notes support one; the HTML title is “{project} v{version} is here” with the release date below. Both HTML and plain text now include TL;DR, highlights, the complete categorized notes, known issues, links, upgrade instructions, and the unsubscribe footer. A rendered v0.5.93 sample is checked in under `docs/release-email-samples/`.

## Work and rationale

The original renderer used a subject based directly on the configured project name and “is out,” then partitioned the notes into broad Features, Fixes, and Other buckets. This was the source of both the awkward “Publish RepoOS” subject and the loss of meaningful categories. I changed the display name resolution to remove the known leading “Publish” release action prefix and made the subject derive from release-note content. If no headline is available, the version-only subject remains clear and professional.

Summary generation is intentionally deterministic. It reads headings, bullet items, and paragraphs already stored in the release history, so it adds no LLM call to either drafting or sending. The helper produces a headline, a concise TL;DR, and up to five distinct highlights. For section prose, the section title supplies the feature name and the opening sentence supplies its explanation; for a “Highlights” list, individual bullets supply their names. Duplicate names are dropped. If notes are missing or cannot produce summary material, the headline and TL;DR are omitted and the full-notes fallback remains available.

The release email record now carries the summary for the version. Sending computes or reuses that value once before iterating recipients, and each personalized message receives the same summary. Existing record writes preserve it, so retries keep the same release copy. Preview reads the stored summary when present and otherwise uses the same deterministic helper. This keeps previews and sends aligned without introducing a separate state store or disrupting recipient-specific unsubscribe URLs.

For the body, the renderer now walks the original Markdown sections in order and retains their headings. It suppresses a heading named “Other” only when that is the sole category. The summary appears above the full notes, preserving complete technical detail below. HTML adds a restrained typographic hierarchy, responsive padding, and a practical dark-mode media query. The multipart text alternative mirrors the same order and existing operational fields. Repository release and changelog links continue to come from the established link resolver.

The sample files are rendered from the repository’s actual `release-history.json` v0.5.93 entry, using the configured release name and upgrade command. The subject in the sample is “RepoOS v0.5.93 released — Task drawer: compact metadata,” and the body summarizes the actual task drawer, review history, Mac Hub, and operator workflow changes in that release.

## Approaches tried

I first reused the existing category bucketing and added summary rendering around it. That retained the original problem: notes with headings such as “Task drawer: compact metadata” would still lose their categories in the full notes section. I replaced the buckets with an ordered section parser that keeps the source headings and body intact.

The first summary extraction pass treated the first heading as the feature name even for bullets under a category heading. The focused tests exposed “Features” as a subject headline. I adjusted extraction so bullets use their own note text, while section titles are used for paragraph-style notes. I also covered the distinction between a lone “Other” heading, which is redundant, and “Other” alongside meaningful categories, which should remain visible.

I initially ran the full required RepoOS check before formatting. Its build and tests completed, but the tests surfaced four old-subject assertions and two summary extraction issues. After correcting those, all 71 release-email tests passed locally. The next check’s remote validation passed, but its local format guard then identified two files needing the repository formatter. I ran `bun run fmt` and repeated the full required check on the formatted tree.

## Challenges and blockers

Remote validation hosts had intermittent Tailscale link-probe failures and the final successful host waited about 95 seconds for an available test slot. RepoOS retried on other hosts and completed validation; this was an infrastructure delay, not a code failure. The first attempted final check was not green because formatting had not yet been applied, so I did not treat that run as completion. The subsequent full check passed.

The notes format is intentionally flexible: some releases use category headings with bullets, while v0.5.93 uses descriptive headings and paragraphs. The extraction helper uses only those stored words and does not attempt to reinterpret implementation details through a model. This keeps content grounded and makes fallback behavior predictable, though the quality of a headline necessarily depends on how clearly the release notes are written.

## Key learnings

Release history already contains enough structured Markdown to create a useful email summary without expanding the release-notes generation pipeline or calling an LLM again. Parsing and retaining the source sections is also a better fit for the full changelog than grouping everything into a fixed set of labels. Keeping a small summary on the per-version email record provides stability across retries while leaving unsubscribe behavior recipient-specific.

Verification completed with `REPOOS_CHECK_CHANGED=main repoos check`: remote build and changed-path tests passed; local formatting, lint, build, CSS/theme guards, rendered contrast, branch-artifact guard, and UI smoke passed. The focused release-email suite passed all 71 tests. The check ran UI smoke at desktop and mobile widths in light and dark mode; the email itself was not sent to a live mailbox or rendered in Gmail, so the checked-in sample is the available visual artifact for review.
